review had to cover slab geometry, poisoning, destruction and ownership, rollback, and
plain-versus-pooled differences. It was not allowed to edit, fix, commit or fabricate, and it
had to stop after the report. The report had five sections: A confirmed, B plausible,
C dismissed, D coverage gaps, E fixes. I wrote the target list deliberately without
pre-dismissing anything, and one of its lines was "pool_destroy called while live objects
remain — whether any such path is legal under the actual API contract".

**What came back.**
- **Confirmed (A):**
  - A1: a reentrant `value_free` that calls back into the tree hits a use-after-free. ASan
    shows it in both modes.
  - A2: 0xDD poisoning never covers the node's `key` field, because the free-list link occupies
    offset 0.
- **Plausible (B):**
  - B1: a build defect.
  - B2: a self-overwrite with the same value pointer.
  - B3: the meaning of `fault_alloc_total`.
  - B4: NULL asserts in the pool.
- **Dismissed (C):** the reviewer investigated the `pool_destroy`-with-live-objects suspicion
  and dismissed it.
- **Coverage gaps (D):**
  - a fault sweep that is too small;
  - no tree-driven pool-invariant check;
  - a fuzzer that never checks links or `rb_foreach`;
  - the REFLECTION.md items still owed.

Every gate (test, asan, stress-asan, memcheck) was green at `4fba98b` when the review ran.

**Genuine finding: B1. I triaged it upward, and my reason differs from the reviewer's.**
`src/rbtree.c:2` and `src/pool.c:28` both said `#include "fault_alloc.h"`. Our Makefile passes
`-Itests`, so the header was found. The reviewer put this in B, "plausible". Its stated reasoning
was an inference: the problem only matters *if* the grader builds with its own command line.
I don't think that "if" is open. Appendix B of the spec documents the build line, and that line
uses `-Iinclude` only. A tree that fails to compile under the spec's own documented flags is
defective against the spec. That holds whatever the grader happens to do. I accepted B1 as
genuine and asked for a plan first: reproduce, show the exact failing command, propose the
minimum correction, and edit nothing yet.

The reproduction was Appendix B's test-binary command, run from the repo root:
`gcc -std=c23 -Wall -Wextra -Werror -g -O1 -Iinclude src/rbtree.c src/pool.c tests/test_rbtree.c tests/fault_alloc.c -o test_rbtree -lpthread`.
It failed with two errors: `src/rbtree.c:2:10: fatal error: fault_alloc.h: No such file or
directory` and the same error at `src/pool.c:28:10`. The fuzz line failed identically. The two
`tests/` files that include the same header compile fine, because a quoted include searches the
including file's own directory first, and the header is in `tests/`.

The fix is two lines, `#include "../tests/fault_alloc.h"`. It was verified on a scratch copy
before I approved it, then applied as `750554e`. Afterwards:
- both Appendix B lines compile warning-free with no `-Itests`;
- `make test`, `make asan`, `make stress-asan` and `make memcheck` all pass from clean builds;
- the count is still 5439 PASS, so nothing silently dropped out;
- valgrind reports 0 errors on all four runs;
- `git diff --check` is clean, and the diff is exactly the two include lines.

I deliberately left the Makefile's `-Itests` in place, because removing it isn't part of the fix.

**False positive: `pool_destroy` with live objects.** This one came from me. I put it in the
prompt because a pooled `rb_destroy` never calls `pool_free`, so the pool is always destroyed
with `live > 0`. Out of context that looks like the classic "freed the allocator out from under
its objects" bug. The reviewer investigated it and dismissed it. I checked that dismissal against
the spec myself rather than taking it on trust. §8.2 says `pool_destroy` releases everything
"regardless of how many objects are live". Destroying with live objects is the documented
contract, not a tolerated edge case. Our design also only does it after the teardown walk has
freed every key and owned value, which are the only things outside the slabs. The episode 8
teardown decision already depended on this. So it is not a defect, and I am recording it as
the false positive because the suspicion was reasonable on its face.

**What I accepted only partly, and what I froze.**
- **A2.** The limitation is real: a stale `key` reads as NULL or `""` rather than as 0xDD
  garbage. I rejected the reviewer's framing that the link placement *violates* the spec.
  §8.2 itself anticipates the free-list link overwriting part of the poisoned bytes. So this is
  a REFLECTION.md item, not a fix.
- **A1.** I accept the ASan reproduction as an observed use-after-free. I left the fix
  unapproved because it turns on a contract question the header doesn't answer: is a
  destructor allowed to re-enter the tree at all? `rb_delete`, `rb_insert`, `pool_free` and
  `pool_destroy` are frozen until I decide that.
- **The gaps (D).** They are legitimate, but I want them scoped before anything grows.

**Judgment.** I accepted one finding as genuine, for my reason rather than the reviewer's
inference. One suspicion was cleared against the spec text. One finding was partly accepted,
and one fix was deliberately deferred. The pattern I'd flag is the reviewer's confidence labels.
B1, the only finding that changed code, was filed as "plausible". A1, which ASan proves, may
turn out to be out of contract. Severity labels from a review are an input to triage, not its
result.

Pool design decisions (HW2 Mutation 2), still to be rewritten in my own words. Each slab is one 4096-byte `rb_malloc` block, and its header is in-band. The header holds only the `next` pointer of the slab chain, so `pool_destroy` saves `next` before it frees each slab. We put the header in-band because it costs no second allocation per slab and no second failure path. The price is that the header 
- `slabs` is the number of slabs obtained;

- `free_objs` is the number of objects `pool_alloc` can still return without calling `rb_malloc`, i.e. free-listed slots plus never-carved slots.

The invariant is `live + free_objs == slabs * objs_per_slab`. Debug builds also walk the free list (with a bound) to cross-check its length, so the invariant isn't checked only against the counters that the mutators maintain. Comparison with the Linux kernel's `kmem_cache` (Bonwick's slab allocator), still to be rewritten in my own words. Like `kmem_cache`, our pool is a cache of fixed-size objects carved out of page-sized slabs, with a free list threaded through the dead objects, and for small objects the kernel also keeps slab management data on the slab itself. The differences:
- the kernel caches *constructed* objects (constructor and destructor callbacks), so a freed object keeps its initialised state; ours keeps no state, and the tree rewrites every field;
- it colours slabs (staggers offsets) to spread objects across cache lines;
- it keeps per-CPU object caches so allocation scales across threads; ours is single-threaded;
- it gives fully free slabs back to the page allocator under memory pressure; ours keeps every slab until `pool_destroy` releases them all at once, which is why whole-tree teardown never calls `pool_free`.

# Handoff audit (read-only; nothing modified, nothing committed)

I ran only inspection commands. I did not re-run `make test`, `make asan` or `make memcheck`. The 5439-PASS figure below comes from the docs, not from this laptop.

## 1. Git state
- **Branch and commit:** `main` at `fe92625`, which is the HEAD you expected. `750554e` (the Appendix B include fix) is its parent.
- **Remote sync:** `main...origin/main` shows no ahead or behind, and `@{u}` equals HEAD.
- **Working tree:** clean. There are no stashes and no other branches.
- **Commit count:** 47 commits in total. The 10-commit requirement is met comfortably, and the history is incremental.
- **Untracked or ignored:** only `build/` is ignored. Everything Git carried over is the committed state, and nothing uncommitted survived from the desktop.

## 2. PROMPTLOG Episode 9
- **Exists:** yes. `PROMPTLOG.md:459` is "HW2 hostile review…", and lines 461–462 carry the DRAFT banner.
- **Content:** it covers the prompt, what came back (A/B/C/D), the B1 reproduction and fix, the `pool_destroy` false positive, A1/A2 handling, and a judgment paragraph. The banner says the evidence and verdicts are final but the prose isn't yet in your own words.
- **Episode count:** 9, inside the required 6–10. The file ends with the "no rejected or oversized diff" note.

## 3. REFLECTION.md
- **Length:** 30 lines, about 1,486 words. The spec says 1–2 pages, so it needs trimming.
- **Drafted material is present:** yes. It sits after a DRAFT comment at line 17.
  - Pool design: in-band slab header, 16-byte alignment, 48-byte stride, 85 slots per slab with zero slack.
  - The three `pool_stats` definitions and the invariant.
  - Poisoning: order, the `key`-at-offset-0 limitation, and `NDEBUG`.
  - The `kmem_cache` comparison.
- **Earlier material, not marked as draft:**
  - most and least reliable;
  - the bug Claude introduced;
  - the surprises as a C newcomer;
  - the parent-pointer cost;
  - the stress-test sizes.
- **Spec checklist (§13):** every required topic is present. The two draft sections still carry the "still to be rewritten in my own words" wording.
- **Not yet in REFLECTION (the plan's own triage list):** the A2 limitation. The Evening 7 balanced-vs-spine control finding is also still owed, per DEVLOG's last OPEN list.

## 4. Raw transcripts

Sessions live in `~/.claude/projects/-home-rauld-cs370-rbtree-lab/`. The repo's `transcripts/` folder is tracked in Git.

| Status | Sessions |
|---|---|
| In repo and identical to the laptop copy | 12 HW1-era `.jsonl` files (Sep 12–16) |
| In repo only, no laptop copy | `da57b840`, `5f60b42b`, `15973812` (Aug–Sep, HW1 era) |
| In repo but stale | `0207446f` — the repo copy lacks the last two lines (`last-prompt`, `cost-state`) |
| HW2, only inside `HW2-transcripts.zip` | `47e7512d`, `25f80ce8`, and `c22503d4` (the zip copy is older than the live one, 585,059 vs 585,766 bytes) |
| HW2, on the laptop only, not in the repo | `a59780c6` (Oct 9–10, about 5 min), `c22503d4` (the newer copy), and the current session `86940087` |

- **Zip is not raw `.jsonl`:** the spec says to copy the raw `.jsonl` files "as-is". A zip of them probably doesn't meet that, so the files need extracting into `transcripts/`.
- **Major gap:** no session on this laptop covers Oct 7–8 (pool slices and pooled integration), Oct 12–13 (Evening 7 and 8, M3), or the Oct 14 hostile review. Commits exist for all of those days. Those `.jsonl` files are almost certainly on the desktop.
  - Episode 9's hostile-review session and the M3 sessions are exactly what the grader will cross-check.
  - Raw transcripts are graded: 2 of the 15 points come from the transcript analysis.
  - The 30-day auto-purge applies, and the desktop's Oct 7 files purge around Nov 6.
- **Odd file:** `003dad60…jsonl` is a 3-line stub with no content, and the `.zip` files in that directory are older exports. Neither is submission material.
- **`cleanupPeriodDays`:** not set in `~/.claude/settings.json` on this laptop.

## 5. Assignment requirements still unsatisfied

**Process deliverables**
1. **Transcripts incomplete.** The HW2 sessions from Oct 7–14 are missing, and the raw `.jsonl` copies of the others are not extracted from the zip.
2. **PROMPTLOG Episode 9 is still DRAFT.** It needs rewriting in your own words and the banner removed.
3. **REFLECTION.md** is over length, and two sections are explicitly marked as not yet in your words.
4. **PROMPTLOG "rejected/oversized diff" requirement.**
   - The spec lists "one rejected/oversized diff (Step 4)" as required, and the log openly says it has none.
   - Episode 7 has a rejected plan element (`src/pool.h`), not a diff.
   - DEVLOG item (h) mentions an "M5 self-vouching hook (rejected diff)" candidate from Evening 7, which Episode 8 may or may not cover. I only grepped for it and didn't read it, so it's worth checking whether that is a real rejected diff.
5. **DEVLOG and CLAUDE.md** have no entry for the Oct 14 session. The last DEVLOG entry is Oct 13, and CLAUDE.md doesn't mention the B1 fix or the hostile review.

**Code and spec**
- **No definite spec violation is known to be open.**
  - B1 is fixed.
  - `pool_destroy` with live objects is allowed by §8.2.
  - A2 is a limitation, not a violation.
  - `rb_snapshot` is ungraded, and per §4/§8.4 it may be left undefined.
- **A1 is undecided** (a reentrant `value_free` causes a use-after-free). It turns on a contract question, and the plan freezes the fix until you decide.
- **B2–B4 are untriaged**, and the three coverage gaps (small fault sweep, no tree-driven pool invariant, fuzzer never checks links or `rb_foreach`) are unscoped.

1. **Recover the missing transcripts from the desktop.** This is the one item I can't fix from here. Copy the Oct 7–14 `.jsonl` files over (a USB drive or `scp` would do).

The heap left-spine case that follows it then died with `AddressSanitizer: stack-overflow ... in rec_free` at both sizes. The abort ends the process, so the pooled cases never ran in the control. So the spec's own required test (a balanced 10^6-node destroy on a 64 KB stack) cannot distinguish recursive from iterative teardown on its own; the hook-built spine is what makes the test discriminating, and even the routine 2·10^4 size catches it. 8:DECIDED: (1) **No production teardown change.** The review and proof found no defect, so pointer reversal was not considered further. (8) **Line-buffered stdout in `--stress` mode only**, because the negative control showed that an ASan abort lost every PASS line when stdout went to a file, so a CI log could not say which case crashed. and `total >= n` with no observed `-1` must fail the test rather than end the sweep.

fixed, finite scenario already guarantees termination by construction — an unbounded `for (n = 1;

*termination condition* and *ownership-on-failure* logic as hard as the production code being
tested — a bug in the harness's own loop can silently mask the exact defect (an API swallowing an
injected failure) the harness exists to catch.

# Episode 9 and rejected-diff audit (read-only; nothing edited)

## 1. Does a rejected/oversized-diff episode exist?

The spec (§13, Step 4) requires "one rejected/oversized diff". Step 4 describes it as a diff that comes back touching too many files and is sent back with "Too big. Insert path only." It also covers an agent quietly weakening tests to make them pass.

**Candidate A: the Evening 7 self-validating spine hook ("M5").** This is the strongest candidate, but I can't confirm it from this laptop.

| Evidence | Where |
|---|---|
| "The reshape never vouches for itself. The first draft had `make_spine` return its own spine length; a 'does nothing, returns n' mutant passed, so measuring moved into a separate `rb_test_spine_len`." | `DEVLOG.md:122`, DECIDED (3) |
| "a test hook that reports on its own work hides its own bugs (mutant M5)" | `DEVLOG.md:123`, LEARNED |
| "PROMPTLOG candidates from tonight: the M5 self-vouching hook (rejected diff), the recursive negative control (tool-output loop), the failed-join race (adversarial finding)" | `DEVLOG.md:125`, OPEN (h) |
| The fix as it exists in the code: "so the reshape never vouches for itself" | `src/rbtree.c:620` and `tests/test_rbtree.c:576`; commit `45f8171` has only the fixed version |

- **Not in PROMPTLOG.** Nothing in `PROMPTLOG.md` covers it, and Episode 8 covers Oct 8 (pool integration), not Oct 12.
- **Transcript missing.** `grep` for "vouch" and `rb_test_make_spine` across `~/.claude/projects/…` finds only the current session. The Oct 12 session isn't on this laptop.
- **Unknown from the docs:**
  - whether the first draft was presented as a diff;
  - who caught it (you, or Claude's mutation run);
  - whether it was sent back or fixed in place.
- **Why it matters:** the DEVLOG label "(rejected diff)" is a candidate note, not evidence. If Claude self-caught it before showing you anything, it doesn't fit Step 4.
- **If the transcript supports it:** it would be a strong episode. It is a hook that tests itself, and a mutant exposed that, which is the spec's "agent weakening tests" failure mode.

**Candidate B: Episode 6, Round 5.** This one is verifiable now but weak.
- Claude had added a 64-iteration cap, `FAULT_SWEEP_MAX_N`. You asked for it to be removed, and Claude removed it in a 3-line diff (`PROMPTLOG.md:299–303`).
- It really was sent back, but it's small, not oversized, and Episode 6 already says "nothing rejected outright."

**Candidate C, ruled out:** the Episode 8 sequencing pushback. The log itself says it isn't one (`PROMPTLOG.md:412–417`, `:451–453`).

**Staleness problem.**
- The closing note (`PROMPTLOG.md:553–564`) says a transcript search found no rejected diff, and calls that "a checked fact".
- That note was written in `8cd7c72` on Oct 8, before Evening 7. It can't have covered the M5 hook, so it's out of date either way.

**My recommendation:** don't decide this until you've checked the Oct 12 transcript on the desktop.
- If the transcript shows a draft shown to you and sent back, add it as Episode 10. That brings the log to 10 episodes, still within 6–10.
- If it was self-caught, tell me which wording you want.
- If neither, the closing note stays but needs rewriting. Candidate B would then be the nearest honest fit, disclosed as small.

## 2. Episode 9 fact check

I checked each point you listed against what's in the repo and spec.

| Claim | Verdict |
|---|---|
| B1 genuine, fixed in `750554e` | **Verified.** The commit changes exactly 2 lines. `src/rbtree.c:2` and `src/pool.c:28` now read `#include "../tests/fault_alloc.h"`. The Makefile has `-Iinclude -Itests`, and Appendix B's starter Makefile has `-Iinclude` only. |
| `pool_destroy` with live objects is the false positive; §8.2 permits it | **Verified.** §8.2 says "pool_destroy frees every slab regardless of how many objects are live". The grading table also lists "pool_destroy safe with live objects". The episode quotes only the first, and you could cite the table too. |
| A1: ASan-reproduced destructor reentrancy, decision unresolved | **Consistent with PLAN.md.** The ASan trace and "both modes" are only in the missing session transcript. |
| A2: a limitation, not a spec violation | **Consistent with the spec.** The spec says "the poison and the 'next' pointer want the same bytes, and only one of them can have them", so the link replacing poisoned bytes is anticipated. |

**Claims I could not verify:** these rest on the review-session transcript, which is on the desktop.
- the exact prompt wording ("fresh session", "named only those sources of truth", the A–E report sections);
- "verified on a scratch copy before I approved it";
- the reviewer's B-section rationale ("only matters if the grader builds with its own command line").

PLAN.md matches the finding names and the triage, so I'd treat these as likely right but worth a spot-check.

**Two details need your attention.**
- **Gap D4.** The episode lists "the REFLECTION.md items still owed" as a coverage gap. PLAN.md's gap list names only the small fault sweep, the missing tree-driven pool invariant, and the fuzzer never checking links or `rb_foreach`. Is D4 really a reviewer finding, or did it come from your own notes? If it isn't from the review, drop it.
- **Reproduction command.** The episode calls it "Appendix B's test-binary command". It is really the expansion of Appendix B's recipe, with `-o test_rbtree` instead of `-o build/test_rbtree`. Calling it "the expansion of Appendix B's recipe" is more exact.

## 3. Proposed edits, factual and structural only

- **E1 (required).** Delete the DRAFT banner at `PROMPTLOG.md:461–462`:
  `> DRAFT (2026-10-14). The evidence and my verdicts below are final. The prose still needs a` / `> pass in my own words before submission.`
- **E2 (accuracy).** Reword "Appendix B of the spec documents the build line, and that line uses `-Iinclude` only" to "Appendix B's starter Makefile sets `CFLAGS` with `-Iinclude` only." Reword "Appendix B's test-binary command" to "the expansion of Appendix B's recipe".
- **E3 (optional addition of a verified fact).** Add one sentence to the A1 bullet: the same gap was already recorded as OPEN (d) in DEVLOG's Evening 7 entry (`DEVLOG.md:125`) and OPEN (c) in Evening 8 (`:135`). The review rediscovered it with ASan evidence, which supports your "may be out of contract" judgment. It's your call, since it adds a fact but no judgment.
- **E4 (confirm first).** Drop or confirm gap D4, per the question above.
- **E5.** Rewrite the closing note (`PROMPTLOG.md:553–564`). The new text depends on the section 1 outcome: either replace it with the new episode or disclosure, or keep it with its stale "checked fact" wording corrected.
- **E6.** Any new episode or intro line that changes the episode count needs a matching update to the header at `PROMPTLOG.md:8` (the line that lists the episodes and their commits).

**Left untouched on purpose:** the Judgment paragraph, the triage verdicts, and your reasoning on B1 and the false positive. All of it checks out. As for prose, the draft is in a tidy, Claude-like register. You said earlier you wanted it in your own words. Do you want me to leave the wording alone and only make the edits above, or is that rewrite something you'll do yourself?

**Before I apply anything, I need two things from you:**
1. The desktop's Oct 12 session `.jsonl` for the M5 hook (and the Oct 14 review session, if you can spot-check the unverified claims).
2. Your answer on D4 and on the E3 sentence.

## 9. HW2 hostile review — a "plausible" build finding I upgraded to genuine, and a suspicion I named myself that the spec rules out

> DRAFT (2026-10-14). The evidence and my verdicts below are final. The prose still needs a
> pass in my own words before submission.

**The prompt.** This was a fresh session with an adversarial review of all the HW2 work: the
pooled tree, `src/pool.c`, the fault injector, and Mutation 3's teardown and traversal. I named
the sources of truth as CS370-HW2.pdf and the frozen `include/rbtree.h`, and only those. The
review had to cover slab geometry, poisoning, destruction and ownership, rollback, and
plain-versus-pooled differences. It was not allowed to edit, fix, commit or fabricate, and it
had to stop after the report. The report had five sections: A confirmed, B plausible,
C dismissed, D coverage gaps, E fixes. I wrote the target list deliberately without
pre-dismissing anything, and one of its lines was "pool_destroy called while live objects
remain — whether any such path is legal under the actual API contract".

**What came back.**
- **Confirmed (A):**
  - A1: a reentrant `value_free` that calls back into the tree hits a use-after-free. ASan
    shows it in both modes.
  - A2: 0xDD poisoning never covers the node's `key` field, because the free-list link occupies
    offset 0.
- **Plausible (B):**

1	Where Claude was the MOST reliable: Claude was most reliable when we were debugging problems using the actual tool output. One example was when make memcheck failed immediately after make asan, reporting that the ASan runtime was not first in the library list. Rather than assuming there was a memory-management bug in my red-black tree, Claude correctly identified that Make had reused an ASan executable beause the source files did not change. It suggested running make clean && make memcheck, which solved the issue and had a clean Valgrind report. When the same problem reappeared, Claude caught it immediately. This showed me that Claude was very useful when it was given concrete error messages and test goals to reason through, even though its workaround did not permanently fix the underlying Makefile issue. 
     2	
     3	Where Claude was the LEAST reliable: While I was determining what work was still required wihtout checking the assignment spec directly. I asked it to identify outsanding tasks, and it found 3 final open items. I challenged them as I realized certain ones such as pool.c or fault_alloc were not part of this assignment. And a test Claude believed to be missing was not required. If I accepted the first response, I would have spent a significant amount of time on unnecessary items. This showed me that Claude's answers even when told to check specifically, must be double checked against constraints and must find what is reasonable rather than what appears to be missing. 
     4	
     5	A bug Claude introduced: Claude originally wrote two tests labeled as red-sibling deletion cases, but the insertion did not actually produce red siblings, rather, it would creat a different red-black-tree configuration, meaning the tests were not executing the proprer deletion-fixup case. 
     6	
     7	I did not initially notice the wrong coloring myself. But before approving the implemetation plan I asked Claude to trace how each test got to its designated deletion case. This prompted Claude to compile and run an instrumented version of the actual implementation, finding tha tits hand-simulated tree colors were incorrect. We then proceeded to replace the two sequences with empirically verified ones and documented the findings.
     8	
     9	This showed me that verification is a non-negotionable rather than assuming test-cases that simply look correct. A test can pass while still failing to execute the statements it supposedly covers, and the verification requirement I adopted allowed us to find the mistake before more progress had happened.
    10	
    11	What surprised me the most as a C newcomer was how pointers worked, while they look simple given they're literally just a -> or a *. It took a while to learn how they really work. I also liked how the syntax isn't too different from Java. I didn't know how important it was nor how memory management worked. I had to understand that it wasn't as easy as just calling free(). I had to find out how to properly have a single stage of freeing in order to avoid a double free or use-after-free. I also had to find out that sometimes it would be simple, such as freely removing red node children.
    12	
    13	The memory cost of the parent pointer (HW2 Mutation 3): our O(1)-space `rb_foreach` walks parent pointers, so the spec asks what that pointer costs. There are three different numbers here, and they shouldn't be confused. The structure size is the first one: measured with `sizeof` on this toolchain (gcc 15.2, x86-64), `struct rb_node` is 48 bytes with the parent pointer and 40 bytes without it. The pool stride is the second: the pool rounds every slot up to `alignof(max_align_t)`, which is 16 bytes here, so both 48 and 40 round to the same 48-byte stride, and a 4096-byte slab holds 85 nodes either way (measured with `rb_pool_geometry`). In pooled mode the parent pointer therefore costs nothing extra right now, but that is an accident of the current layout and alignment, not something the design guarantees. The third number is the heap allocation size, which depends on the allocator implementation rather than on our code: in ordinary mode each node is its own `malloc`, and glibc 2.43 reported a usable size of 56 bytes for the 48-byte node and 40 bytes for the 40-byte one. That is a 16-byte difference in the usable allocation size per node, not a measurement of 16 bytes of allocator overhead: what glibc spends on bookkeeping around each chunk is a separate question, and these figures are specific to this glibc version and platform; another allocator could round differently. Key copies are separate allocations and aren't affected. `pool_stats` counts objects, not bytes, and the pool's object size is `sizeof(struct rb_node)`, which already includes the pointer, so no change was needed there. We kept the pointer because it was already there since HW1 (deletion fixup depends on it) and because the alternative, Morris traversal, writes into the tree during a read-only walk.
    14	
    15	Stress-test sizes: the spec's million-node requirement is met under AddressSanitizer/UBSan, not under valgrind. `make stress-asan` runs `test_rbtree --stress 1000000`, which builds a 10^6-node tree, balanced and as a single left spine, in both heap and pooled mode, and runs `rb_foreach` and then `rb_destroy` on a thread with a 64 KB stack. Valgrind is many times slower, so `make memcheck` routinely runs the same harness at 20,000 nodes (`--stress 20000`), and `make test`/`make asan` run that 20,000-node size too. This is a deliberate shrink for runtime, made so `make memcheck` still finishes quickly, and it is only for valgrind. The million-node case itself is not shrunk: it is opt-in behind its own target (`make stress-asan`) rather than part of `make test`, so it runs when that target is invoked, not on every build. The 20,000-node size is still big enough to catch recursion: the recursive `rb_foreach` overflowed the 64 KB stack on the 20,000-node left spine and AddressSanitizer reported it as a stack overflow in `foreach_inorder`.
    16	
    17	<!-- DRAFT (2026-10-14): the facts below are checked against src/pool.c; the prose still needs rewriting in my own words, and the whole file needs trimming to the 1–2 page limit. -->
    18	
    19	Pool design decisions (HW2 Mutation 2), still to be rewritten in my own words. Each slab is one 4096-byte `rb_malloc` block, and its header is in-band. The header holds only the `next` pointer of the slab chain, so `pool_destroy` saves `next` before it frees each slab. We put the header in-band because it costs no second allocation per slab and no second failure path. The price is that the header uses part of the slab. Slots are aligned to `alignof(max_align_t)`, which is 16 bytes here, because the pool doesn't know what type it is storing. So the first slot starts at offset 16, not at 8, and the stride is rounded up to a multiple of 16, giving 48 bytes for the 48-byte node. That leaves 4080 bytes, which hold 85 slots with zero slack. The common bug here is computing the slot count from 4096 instead of from what is left after the header. `pool_stats` reports three numbers:
    20	- `slabs` is the number of slabs obtained;
    21	- `live` is the number of objects handed out and not yet freed;
    22	- `free_objs` is the number of objects `pool_alloc` can still return without calling `rb_malloc`, i.e. free-listed slots plus never-carved slots.
    23	
    24	The invariant is `live + free_objs == slabs * objs_per_slab`. Debug builds also walk the free list (with a bound) to cross-check its length, so the invariant isn't checked only against the counters that the mutators maintain. On poisoning: `pool_free` fills the whole slot with 0xDD and then writes the free-list link at offset 0. The order matters, because poisoning after the link would destroy the list. Since `key` is the node's first field, a stale `key` read from a dead slot shows the link (NULL or another dead slot) and not 0xDD. The spec expects the link to take some of the poisoned bytes. The hostile review pointed out that the field it takes is exactly the one a stale search would read. Poisoning is compiled out with `-DNDEBUG`, the same switch as `assert`.
    25	
    26	Comparison with the Linux kernel's `kmem_cache` (Bonwick's slab allocator), still to be rewritten in my own words. Like `kmem_cache`, our pool is a cache of fixed-size objects carved out of page-sized slabs, with a free list threaded through the dead objects, and for small objects the kernel also keeps slab management data on the slab itself. The differences:
    27	- the kernel caches *constructed* objects (constructor and destructor callbacks), so a freed object keeps its initialised state; ours keeps no state, and the tree rewrites every field;
    28	- it colours slabs (staggers offsets) to spread objects across cache lines;
    29	- it keeps per-CPU object caches so allocation scales across threads; ours is single-threaded;
    30	- it gives fully free slabs back to the page allocator under memory pressure; ours keeps every slab until `pool_destroy` releases them all at once, which is why whole-tree teardown never calls `pool_free`.

    17	<!-- DRAFT (2026-10-14): the facts below are checked against src/pool.c; the prose still needs rewriting in my own words, and the whole file needs trimming to the 1–2 page limit. -->
    18	
    19	Pool design decisions (HW2 Mutation 2), still to be rewritten in my own words. Each slab is one 4096-byte `rb_malloc` block, and its header is in-band. The header holds only the `next` pointer of the slab chain, so `pool_destroy` saves `next` before it frees each slab. We put the header in-band because it costs no second allocation per slab and no second failure path. The price is that the header uses part of the slab. Slots are aligned to `alignof(max_align_t)`, which is 16 bytes here, because the pool doesn't know what type it is storing. So the first slot starts at offset 16, not at 8, and the stride is rounded up to a multiple of 16, giving 48 bytes for the 48-byte node. That leaves 4080 bytes, which hold 85 slots with zero slack. The common bug here is computing the slot count from 4096 instead of from what is left after the header. `pool_stats` reports three numbers:
    20	- `slabs` is the number of slabs obtained;
    21	- `live` is the number of objects handed out and not yet freed;
    22	- `free_objs` is the number of objects `pool_alloc` can still return without calling `rb_malloc`, i.e. free-listed slots plus never-carved slots.
    23	
    24	The invariant is `live + free_objs == slabs * objs_per_slab`. Debug builds also walk the free list (with a bound) to cross-check its length, so the invariant isn't checked only against the counters that the mutators maintain. On poisoning: `pool_free` fills the whole slot with 0xDD and then writes the free-list link at offset 0. The order matters, because poisoning after the link would destroy the list. Since `key` is the node's first field, a stale `key` read from a dead slot shows the link (NULL or another dead slot) and not 0xDD. The spec expects the link to take some of the poisoned bytes. The hostile review pointed out that the field it takes is exactly the one a stale search would read. Poisoning is compiled out with `-DNDEBUG`, the same switch as `assert`.
    25	
    26	Comparison with the Linux kernel's `kmem_cache` (Bonwick's slab allocator), still to be rewritten in my own words. Like `kmem_cache`, our pool is a cache of fixed-size objects carved out of page-sized slabs, with a free list threaded through the dead objects, and for small objects the kernel also keeps slab management data on the slab itself. The differences:
    27	- the kernel caches *constructed* objects (constructor and destructor callbacks), so a freed object keeps its initialised state; ours keeps no state, and the tree rewrites every field;
    28	- it colours slabs (staggers offsets) to spread objects across cache lines;
    29	- it keeps per-CPU object caches so allocation scales across threads; ours is single-threaded;
    30	- it gives fully free slabs back to the page allocator under memory pressure; ours keeps every slab until `pool_destroy` releases them all at once, which is why whole-tree teardown never calls `pool_free`.

content.text:
# REFLECTION.md editorial audit (read-only)

I touched nothing in the repo. For the measurement check, I compiled a scratch program in the session scratchpad and read `src/pool.c`, the Makefile, DEVLOG and the spec text (§8.2, §8.3, §13).

## 1. Requirement coverage (§13: "1–2 pages")

| §13 requirement | Where it is now | Status |
|---|---|---|
| Slab comparison (kmem_cache) | ¶26–30 | **Partial.** The spec says "one paragraph" and "do not merely list features; ask why they become useful at kernel scale". Ours is a bullet list of 4 features and only some of the *why*. |
| COW comparison "if attempted" | none | `rb_snapshot` was not attempted. One sentence saying so would make that explicit. |
| `pool_stats` definitions | ¶19–24 | ✅ |
| Slab-header decision | ¶19 | ✅ In-band, with its reason and cost. |
| Alignment decision | ¶19 | ✅ `max_align_t` = 16, stride rounded up. |
| Where the agent was most reliable | ¶1 | ✅ (your words) |
| Where the agent was least reliable | ¶3 | ✅ (your words) |
| A bug Claude introduced, how you caught it | ¶5, 7, 9 | ✅ (your words) |
| Poisoning rationale | ¶24 | **Partial.** It covers the ordering, the `key` limitation and `NDEBUG`. It never says what class of bug poisoning catches that ASan cannot: the spec's point that ASan sees the whole slab as live memory. |
| Parent-pointer memory cost (§8.3: "account for in `pool_stats` and your reflection") | ¶13 | ✅ Complete, but about 3× longer than needed. |
| Million-node size disclosure (§7/§8: say so if you shrink it) | ¶15 | ✅ |
| Balanced-vs-spine recursive negative control | none | **Missing.** DEVLOG Evening 7 lists it as owed in two places. |
| Your C-newcomer surprise | ¶11 | ✅ (your words) |

## 2. Duplication, length, draft language
- **Draft markers:** the HTML comment at line 17, "still to be rewritten in my own words" (¶19), and the same phrase on the kmem paragraph (¶26).
- **Parent pointer (¶13, 295 words):** it narrates the same three numbers twice, and the glibc caveat runs long. The "16-byte difference, not a measurement of 16 bytes of overhead" point is good but can be one sentence.
- **Duplicated numbers:** the 48-byte stride and 85-slot figures appear in both ¶13 and ¶19. Say them once.
- **Stress sizes (¶15):** "not shrunk" and "opt-in" are said three ways.
- **Word counts by author:**
  - your six paragraphs: about 515 words;
  - the Claude-drafted technical paragraphs: about 940 words;
  - the draft sections are where nearly all the cuts come from.

## 3. Paragraph-by-paragraph plan

| ¶ | Now | Plan | Target |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 132 | Keep your narrative. Fix the outdated Makefile claim (see contradiction C1) and trim. | ~105 |
| 3 | 114 | Keep. Add a qualifier for the pool.c/fault_alloc claim (C2), once you tell me which assignment it refers to. | ~100 |
| 5, 7, 9 | 155 | Light trims only, no changes in meaning. | ~135 |
| 11 | 114 | Keep as is. One sentence ("simple, such as freely removing red node children") is unclear to a reader, so I'll flag it for you instead of touching it. | ~110 |
| 13 | 295 | Compress to four facts: sizeof 48 vs 40, same 48-byte stride, so 85 slots either way, and the pool cost is "free by alignment luck, not by design". Add one sentence on `malloc` usable size 56 vs 40, labelled as glibc-specific. Add the Morris reason. | ~120 |
| 15 | 165 | Merge with the new negative-control result (below) under "testing limitations". | ~150 |
| 19–24 | 340 | Merge into one pool section: header/alignment/slack, the three stats and the invariant, and the poisoning rationale. This is where I add the missing "what ASan can't see" sentence. | ~230 |
| 26–30 | 150 | One paragraph, with the *why* attached to each feature (constructors, colouring, per-CPU caches, slab reclaim under pressure). | ~110 |
| new | n/a | One sentence: `rb_snapshot` was not attempted, so no COW comparison. | ~15 |

**Negative-control wording, from DEVLOG Evening 7 (scratch copy only, not committed):**
- A textbook recursive `rb_destroy` **passed** the balanced case at both N = 2·10^4 and N = 10^6, because the height is about 40.
- The heap **left-spine case then died** with an ASan stack-overflow in `rec_free` at both sizes. So the spec's own balanced test cannot tell recursive from iterative teardown, and the hook-built spine is what makes it discriminate.
- Separately, the recursive `rb_foreach` overflowed the same 64 KB stack on the left spine in Evening 8 (segfault under `make test`; ASan named `foreach_inorder`). That is the existing ¶15 claim, and DEVLOG supports it.

**Optional (~60 words):** one limitations sentence pointing to Episode 9: A1's contract question is open, A2 means the `key` field isn't poisoned, and D4 means there's no poison check on reuse. These are already decisions on record, but I'd only add it if there's room.

**Estimated total: about 1,000–1,080 words** (down from 1,486), which fits two pages at ordinary single-spaced size.

## 4. Measured vs inferred

**Measured:**
- `sizeof` 48 (with parent) and 40 (without), plus `malloc_usable_size` 56 and 40. I re-ran these just now on this laptop (gcc 15.2.0, glibc 2.43) and got the same numbers as the draft.
- The 85-slot figure follows from the geometry arithmetic and is covered by the geometry unit test. I haven't re-run it.
- The negative-control results and the Evening 8 red-run stack overflow are recorded in DEVLOG, but the sessions are scratch-only.
- ASan at 10^6 passes in about 6 s per DEVLOG.

**Inferred or general knowledge, not measured:**
- the `kmem_cache` feature list (constructors, colouring, per-CPU caches, slab reclaim);
- "the common bug is computing slots from 4096", which is the spec's framing and not something you hit;
- "this accident of layout isn't guaranteed", which is arithmetic-backed but unproven by experiment.

I'd label the kmem points as background knowledge in the edit, not as findings.

## 5. Contradictions found

- **C1: outdated Makefile claim.** ¶1 says the workaround "did not permanently fix the underlying Makefile issue." The Makefile now has `memcheck: clean`, added in commit `bdbb900` ("serialize sanitizer and memcheck rebuilds"). The statement was true when you wrote it and is false now.
- **C2: pool.c / fault_alloc "not part of this assignment" (¶3).**
  - HW2 §7.1 explicitly adds `tests/fault_alloc.c`, `.h` and `src/pool.c`.
  - The claim only holds in an HW1 context.
  - A reader of an HW2 REFLECTION will see a contradiction. Which assignment was that exchange in?
- **C3: stale-key wording differs between Episode 9 and REFLECTION.**
  - Episode 9's A2 bullet (committed in `1d09840`) says a stale `key` reads as "NULL or `""`".
  - ¶24 says "NULL or another dead slot".
  - `pool_free` writes `p->free_head` at offset 0, which is NULL or the address of another dead slot. So ¶24 matches the code, and the `""` in Episode 9 is imprecise.
  - I won't touch Episode 9 without your word. It would be a one-phrase fix in a later commit.
- **C4: valgrind and the million-node case.**
  - ¶15 says the million-node requirement is met "under ASan, not under valgrind". DEVLOG Evening 7 records a one-off scratch valgrind run of the full 10^6 case that was also clean (about 8.5 s heap).
  - It isn't a Makefile target, so the draft isn't wrong. It just omits that fact, and "ASan only" should say "as a gate".
- **C5: page-limit wording.** DEVLOG's Evening 8 OPEN list says "~1 page target". The spec says 1–2 pages, and the spec governs.

**Typos in your paragraphs:** wihtout, outsanding, beause, creat, proprer, implemetation, "tha tits", non-negotionable. Do you want me to fix spelling only, with no wording changes?

**Decisions I need from you before editing:**
1. Which assignment was the pool.c/fault_alloc exchange in (C2)?
2. Spelling-only fixes in your paragraphs: yes or no?
3. Include the optional limitations sentence?
4. Fix Episode 9's "`""`" wording (C3) in a separate small commit, or leave it?

**Where Claude was the MOST reliable:** when we debugged from actual tool output. `make memcheck` failed right after `make asan`, reporting that the ASan runtime was not first in the library list. Rather than assuming a memory bug in my red-black tree, Claude correctly saw that Make had reused an ASan executable because the sources had not changed, and suggested `make clean && make memcheck`, which gave a clean Valgrind report. When the same problem reappeared, Claude caught it immediately. That workaround did not fix the Makefile at the time; the fix came later in commit `bdbb900`, which made `memcheck` rebuild from clean. The lesson I took is that Claude is very useful when it is given concrete error messages and test goals to reason through.

**Where Claude was the LEAST reliable:** when I asked what work was still required without checking the assignment spec directly. It reported three open items. I challenged them because two were not required by the HW1 spec: `pool.c` and `fault_alloc` were later-assignment material already in the repo, and a test Claude believed was missing was not required (PROMPTLOG Episode 5). Had I accepted the first answer, I would have spent significant time on unnecessary work. Claude's answers, even when told to check, must be verified against the constraints.

**A bug Claude introduced:** Claude wrote two tests labeled as red-sibling deletion cases, but the insertion sequences did not actually produce red siblings. They produced a different red-black configuration, so the tests were not exercising the intended deletion-fixup case. I did not notice the wrong coloring myself. Before approving the implementation plan I asked Claude to trace how each test reached its designated case. It compiled and ran an instrumented copy of the real implementation and found its hand-simulated colors were wrong. We replaced the two sequences with empirically verified ones and documented the finding. This showed me that verification is non-negotiable: a test can pass without executing the statements it is named for, and requiring the trace caught the mistake before more work was built on it.

**As a C newcomer,** what surprised me most was how pointers work. They look simple, since they are just `->` or `*`, but it took a while to learn how they really work. I also liked that the syntax is not too different from Java. I did not know how much memory management matters, or that it is not as easy as calling `free()`; I had to learn to give every allocation a single place where it is freed, to avoid double frees and use-after-free. I also found that some cases are simple, such as freely removing red node children.

**Pool design (Mutation 2).** Each slab is one 4096-byte `rb_malloc` block with an in-band header holding only the slab-chain `next` pointer, so there is no second allocation and no second failure path; the price is that the header takes bytes from the slab. Slots are aligned to `alignof(max_align_t)` (16 bytes here) because the pool does not know what it stores and a dead slot must also hold the free-list pointer. The header rounds up to 16, so the first slot starts at offset 16, the stride is 48, and (4096 − 16) / 48 gives 85 slots with zero tail slack; the count comes from what remains after the header, not from 4096. `pool_stats` reports `slabs` (slabs obtained), `live` (objects handed out and not yet freed) and `free_objs` (objects `pool_alloc` can return without calling `rb_malloc`: free-listed plus never-carved slots). The invariant is `live + free_objs == slabs * objs_per_slab`; debug builds also walk the free list, with a bound, so the invariant is not checked only against counters the mutators maintain.

**Poisoning.** `pool_free` fills the whole stride with 0xDD and then writes the free-list link at offset 0; the order matters, since the reverse would overwrite the link. A freed node stays inside a live 4096-byte slab, so ASan treats a stale pointer into it as valid memory and reports nothing. Poison makes a stale read of a dead slot return conspicuous 0xDD fields instead of the old node. It does not detect writes to a dead slot, and poison is not verified when a slot is reused (hostile-review gap D4). The link also occupies `key`, the first field, so a stale `key` holds the link pointer (NULL or another dead slot), not 0xDD (finding A2; §8.2 anticipates the link taking some of the poisoned bytes). Poisoning is compiled out by `-DNDEBUG`, like `assert`.

**Comparison with `kmem_cache`.** Our pool is the same core idea as the kernel's slab allocator (Bonwick): fixed-size objects carved from page-sized slabs, with a free list threaded through the dead objects. What the kernel adds comes from general knowledge of Linux, not from anything measured here. It caches *constructed* objects, so freed objects keep their initialised state and frequently used kinds avoid re-initialisation, while ours rewrites every field. It colours slabs by staggering the first slot, so same-index objects from different slabs do not all land on the same cache lines. It keeps per-CPU caches, so many cores can allocate and free one kind of object without contending on one lock or free list, a problem a single-threaded pool never meets. And it returns fully free slabs under memory pressure, because a kernel must give memory back to everything else, whereas ours keeps every slab until `pool_destroy` frees them all at once, which is why whole-tree teardown never calls `pool_free`. `rb_snapshot` (copy-on-write, Mutation 4) was not attempted, since it is optional and ungraded, so there is no COW comparison.

**Parent-pointer cost (Mutation 3).** Our O(1)-space `rb_foreach` walks parent pointers; Morris traversal was rejected because it rewrites `right` links during a read-only walk. Measured with `sizeof` (gcc 15.2, x86-64), `struct rb_node` is 48 bytes with the parent pointer and 40 without. The pool rounds slots up to 16 bytes, so both sizes give a 48-byte stride and 85 nodes per slab (measured with `rb_pool_geometry`): in pooled mode the pointer costs nothing, but that is an accident of this layout, not a guarantee. In ordinary mode each node is its own `malloc`, and glibc 2.43's `malloc_usable_size` reports 56 bytes for the 48-byte node and 40 for the 40-byte one. That is usable size only; glibc's per-chunk bookkeeping was not measured, and another allocator could differ. `pool_stats` counts objects, not bytes, so it needed no change. We kept the pointer because it has existed since HW1 and deletion fixup depends on it.

**Testing limits.** `make stress-asan` runs `test_rbtree --stress 1000000`: a 10^6-node tree, balanced and as one left spine, in heap and pooled mode, with `rb_foreach` and `rb_destroy` on a 64 KB thread stack. The routine Valgrind gate (`make memcheck`) uses 20,000 nodes because Valgrind is many times slower; `make test` and `make asan` also run the 20,000-node case. That shrink is deliberate and applies only to Valgrind. DEVLOG records a one-off scratch Valgrind run of the full 10^6 case that was also clean, but it is not a Makefile target.

The stress test does not detect recursion on its own. In a scratch copy (not committed), `rb_destroy` was replaced with a textbook recursive free and run under ASan. In heap mode the balanced tree passed at both 20,000 and 10^6 nodes, because a red-black tree's height is only about 40. The left spine, built by a test hook that reshapes the tree with the real rotations, then died with an ASan stack overflow at both sizes. The abort ended the run before the pooled cases, so this control was observed in heap mode only. The spec's balanced 10^6 test therefore cannot tell recursive teardown from iterative; the spine can. The old recursive `rb_foreach` likewise overflowed the 64 KB stack on the 20,000-node left spine before the parent-pointer rewrite.

One open question: whether a `value_free` callback may re-enter the tree is an undecided contract question; ASan reproduces a use-after-free there (PROMPTLOG Episode 9, A1).

Rather than assuming a memory bug in my red-black tree, Claude correctly saw that Make had reused an ASan executable because the sources had not changed, and suggested `make clean && make memcheck`, which gave a clean Valgrind report. When the same problem reappeared, Claude caught it immediately. That workaround did not fix the Makefile at the time; the fix came later in commit `bdbb900`, which made `memcheck` rebuild from clean. The lesson I took is that Claude is very useful when it is given concrete error messages and test goals to reason through.

**Where Claude was the LEAST reliable:** when I asked what work was still required without checking the assignment spec directly. It reported three open items. I challenged them because two were not required by the HW1 spec: `pool.c` and `fault_alloc` were later-assignment material already in the repo, and a test Claude believed was missing was not required (PROMPTLOG Episode 5). Had I accepted the first answer, I would have spent significant time on unnecessary work. Claude's answers, even when told to check, must be verified against the constraints.

**A bug Claude introduced:** Claude wrote two tests labeled as red-sibling deletion cases, but the insertion sequences did not actually produce red siblings. They produced a different red-black configuration, so the tests were not exercising the intended deletion-fixup case. I did not notice the wrong coloring myself. Before approving the implementation plan I asked Claude to trace how each test reached its designated case. It compiled and ran an instrumented copy of the real implementation and found its hand-simulated colors were wrong. We replaced the two sequences with empirically verified ones and documented the finding. This showed me that verification is non-negotiable: a test can pass without executing the statements it is named for, and requiring the trace caught the mistake before more work was built on it.

**As a C newcomer,** what surprised me most was how pointers work. They look simple, since they are just `->` or `*`, but it took a while to learn how they really work. I also liked that the syntax is not too different from Java. I did not know how much memory management matters, or that it is not as easy as calling `free()`; I had to learn to give every allocation a single place where it is freed, to avoid double frees and use-after-free. I also found that some cases are simple, such as freely removing red node children.

**Pool design (Mutation 2).** Each slab is one 4096-byte `rb_malloc` block with an in-band header holding only the slab-chain `next` pointer: no second allocation and no second failure path, at the price of header bytes. Slots are aligned to `alignof(max_align_t)` (16 here) because the pool does not know what it stores and a dead slot must also hold the free-list pointer. The header rounds up to 16, so the first slot is at offset 16, the stride is 48, and (4096 − 16) / 48 gives 85 slots with no tail slack; the count comes from what is left after the header, not from 4096. `pool_stats` reports `slabs` (slabs obtained), `live` (handed out, not yet freed) and `free_objs` (what `pool_alloc` can return without calling `rb_malloc`: free-listed plus never-carved slots), with the invariant `live + free_objs == slabs * objs_per_slab`. Debug builds also walk the free list, with a bound, to cross-check it.

**Poisoning.** `pool_free` fills the whole stride with 0xDD, then writes the free-list link at offset 0; the reverse order would overwrite the link. A freed node stays inside a live slab, so ASan treats a stale pointer into it as valid memory and reports nothing; poison makes a stale read of a dead slot see 0xDD fields instead of the old node. It does not detect writes to a dead slot, and poison is not verified on reuse (hostile-review gap D4). The link also occupies `key`, the first field, so a stale `key` holds the link pointer (NULL or another dead slot), not 0xDD (A2; §8.2 anticipates the link taking some poisoned bytes). Poisoning is compiled out by `-DNDEBUG`.

**Comparison with `kmem_cache`.** Same core idea as the kernel's slab allocator (Bonwick): fixed-size objects in page-sized slabs, with a free list threaded through dead objects. The kernel's additions below are general knowledge, not measured here. It caches constructed objects, so frequently used kinds skip re-initialisation, while ours rewrites every field. It colours slabs by staggering the first slot, so same-index objects from different slabs avoid the same cache lines. It keeps per-CPU caches, so many cores can allocate one kind of object without contending on a lock, a problem a single-threaded pool never meets. And it returns fully free slabs under memory pressure, because a kernel must give memory back, whereas ours keeps every slab until `pool_destroy`, which is why whole-tree teardown never calls `pool_free`. `rb_snapshot` (COW, Mutation 4) was not attempted (optional, ungraded), so there is no COW comparison.

**Parent-pointer cost (Mutation 3).** Our O(1)-space `rb_foreach` walks parent pointers; Morris traversal was rejected because it rewrites `right` links during a read-only walk. Measured with `sizeof` (gcc 15.2, x86-64): `struct rb_node` is 48 bytes with the pointer, 40 without. Pool slots round up to 16, so both give a 48-byte stride and 85 nodes per slab (measured with `rb_pool_geometry`): in pooled mode the pointer is free, by accident of layout rather than by design. In ordinary mode glibc 2.43's `malloc_usable_size` reports 56 bytes for the 48-byte node and 40 for the 40-byte one; that is usable size only, not glibc's per-chunk bookkeeping, and another allocator could differ. `pool_stats` counts objects, so it needed no change. We kept the pointer because it has existed since HW1 and deletion fixup depends on it.

**Testing limits.** `make stress-asan` runs `test_rbtree --stress 1000000`: a 10^6-node tree, balanced and as one left spine, heap and pooled, with `rb_foreach` and `rb_destroy` on a 64 KB thread stack. The routine Valgrind gate (`make memcheck`) uses 20,000 nodes because Valgrind is much slower; that shrink is deliberate and Valgrind-only. DEVLOG records a one-off scratch Valgrind run of the full 10^6 case that was also clean, but it is not a Makefile target.

The stress test alone does not detect recursion. In a scratch copy (not committed), `rb_destroy` was replaced with a textbook recursive free and run under ASan. In heap mode the balanced tree passed at 20,000 and 10^6 nodes (a red-black tree's height is about 40); the left spine, built by a test hook using the real rotations, then overflowed the stack at both sizes. The abort ended the run before the pooled cases, so the control was observed in heap mode only. The old recursive `rb_foreach` likewise overflowed on the 20,000-node spine before the parent-pointer rewrite.

Open: whether a `value_free` callback may re-enter the tree is an undecided contract question; ASan reproduces a use-after-free there (PROMPTLOG Episode 9, A1).

CHECK-OK
 M REFLECTION.md
**Where Claude was the MOST reliable:** when we debugged from actual tool output. `make memcheck` failed right after `make asan`, reporting that the ASan runtime was not first in the library list. Rather than assuming a memory bug in my red-black tree, Claude correctly saw that Make had reused an ASan executable because the sources had not changed, and suggested `make clean && make memcheck`, which gave a clean Valgrind report. When the same problem reappeared, Claude caught it immediately. The workaround did not fix the Makefile at the time; commit `bdbb900` later made `memcheck` rebuild from clean. Claude is most useful with concrete error messages.

**Where Claude was the LEAST reliable:** when I asked what work was still required without checking the assignment spec directly. It reported three open items. Two were not required by the HW1 spec: `pool.c` and `fault_alloc` were later-assignment material already in the repo, and a test Claude believed was missing was not required (PROMPTLOG Episode 5). Accepting the first answer would have cost significant time on unnecessary work; even when told to check, Claude's answers must be verified against the constraints.

**A bug Claude introduced:** Claude wrote two tests labeled as red-sibling deletion cases, but the insertion sequences did not actually produce red siblings. They produced a different configuration, so the tests were not exercising the intended fixup case. I did not notice this myself. Before approving the implementation plan I asked Claude to trace how each test reached its designated case. It ran an instrumented copy of the real implementation and found its hand-simulated colors were wrong, and we replaced the two sequences with verified ones. This showed me that verification is non-negotiable: a test can pass without executing the statements it is named for.

**As a C newcomer,** what surprised me most was how pointers work. They look simple, since they are just `->` or `*`, but it took a while to learn how they really work. I also liked that the syntax is not too different from Java. I did not know that memory management is not as easy as calling `free()`; every allocation needs a single place where it is freed, to avoid double frees and use-after-free. I also found that some cases are simple, such as deleting a red leaf, which needs no deletion fixup.

**Pool design (Mutation 2).** Each slab is one 4096-byte `rb_malloc` block with an in-band header (just the slab-chain `next` pointer): no second allocation or failure path, at the price of header bytes. Slots are aligned to `alignof(max_align_t)` (16 here) because the pool does not know what it stores and a dead slot must also hold the free-list pointer. The header rounds up to 16, so the first slot is at offset 16, the stride is 48, and (4096 − 16) / 48 gives 85 slots with no slack; the count uses what is left after the header, not 4096. `pool_stats` reports `slabs` (slabs obtained), `live` (handed out, not yet freed) and `free_objs` (what `pool_alloc` can return without calling `rb_malloc`: free-listed plus never-carved slots), with the invariant `live + free_objs == slabs * objs_per_slab`. In debug builds `pool_stats` also walks the free list, with a bound, to cross-check its length.

**Poisoning.** `pool_free` fills the whole stride with 0xDD, then writes the free-list link at offset 0; the reverse order would overwrite the link. A freed node stays inside a live slab, so ASan treats a stale pointer into it as valid and reports nothing; poison makes a stale read see 0xDD instead of the old node. It does not detect writes to a dead slot, and poison is not verified on reuse (hostile-review gap D4). The link also occupies `key`, the first field, so a stale `key` holds the link pointer (NULL or another dead slot), not 0xDD (A2; §8.2 anticipates this). It is compiled out by `-DNDEBUG`.

**Comparison with `kmem_cache`.** Same core idea as the kernel's slab allocator (Bonwick): fixed-size objects in page-sized slabs, with a free list through dead objects. The additions below are general knowledge, not measured here. The kernel caches constructed objects, so common kinds skip re-initialisation; ours rewrites every field. Traditional slab allocators colour slabs by staggering the first slot so same-index objects avoid the same cache lines (not every modern Linux slab implementation does). Per-CPU caches let many cores allocate one kind of object without contending on a lock, which a single-threaded pool never faces. And it returns free slabs under memory pressure, because a kernel must give memory back; ours keeps every slab until `pool_destroy`, which is why whole-tree teardown never calls `pool_free`. `rb_snapshot` (COW, Mutation 4) was not attempted (optional, ungraded), so there is no COW comparison.

**Parent-pointer cost (Mutation 3).** Our O(1)-space `rb_foreach` walks parent pointers; Morris traversal was rejected because it rewrites `right` links during a read-only walk. By `sizeof` (gcc 15.2, x86-64), `struct rb_node` is 48 bytes with the pointer, 40 without. Slots round up to 16, so both give a 48-byte stride and 85 nodes per slab (measured with `rb_pool_geometry`): in pooled mode the pointer is free, by accident of layout rather than design. In ordinary mode glibc 2.43's `malloc_usable_size` reports 56 bytes for the 48-byte node and 40 for the 40-byte one; that is usable size only, not glibc's per-chunk bookkeeping, and another allocator could differ. `pool_stats` counts objects, so it needed no change. We kept the pointer because deletion fixup has depended on it since HW1.

**Testing limits.** `make stress-asan` runs 10^6 nodes, balanced and as one left spine, heap and pooled, with `rb_foreach` and `rb_destroy` on a 64 KB thread stack. The routine Valgrind gate (`make memcheck`) uses 20,000 nodes because Valgrind is much slower; that shrink is deliberate. DEVLOG records a one-off scratch Valgrind run of the full 10^6 case that was also clean, but it is not a Makefile target.

The balanced million-node stress test alone cannot detect the recursive-stack problem; the adversarial left spine does. In a scratch copy (not committed), `rb_destroy` was replaced with a textbook recursive free and run under ASan. In heap mode the balanced tree passed at 20,000 and 10^6 nodes (a red-black tree's height is about 40), while the left spine, built by a test hook using the real rotations, overflowed the 64 KB stack at both sizes. The abort ended the run before the pooled cases, so the control was observed in heap mode only.

In debug builds `pool_stats` also walks the free list, with a bound, to cross-check its length.

**Poisoning.** `pool_free` fills the whole stride with 0xDD, then writes the free-list link at offset 0; the reverse order would overwrite the link. A freed node stays inside a live slab, so ASan treats a stale pointer into it as valid and reports nothing; poison makes a stale read see 0xDD instead of the old node. It does not detect writes to a dead slot, and poison is not verified on reuse (hostile-review gap D4). The link also occupies `key`, the first field, so a stale `key` holds the link pointer (NULL or another dead slot), not 0xDD (A2; §8.2 anticipates this). It is compiled out by `-DNDEBUG`.

**Comparison with `kmem_cache`.** Same core idea as the kernel's slab allocator (Bonwick): fixed-size objects in page-sized slabs, with a free list through dead objects. The additions below are general knowledge, not measured here. The kernel caches constructed objects, so common kinds skip re-initialisation; ours rewrites every field. Traditional slab allocators colour slabs by staggering the first slot so same-index objects avoid the same cache lines (not every modern Linux slab implementation does). Per-CPU caches let many cores allocate one kind of object without contending on a lock, which a single-threaded pool never faces. And it returns free slabs under memory pressure, because a kernel must give memory back; ours keeps every slab until `pool_destroy`, which is why whole-tree teardown never calls `pool_free`. `rb_snapshot` (COW, Mutation 4) was not attempted (optional, ungraded), so there is no COW comparison.

**Parent-pointer cost (Mutation 3).** Our O(1)-space `rb_foreach` walks parent pointers; Morris traversal was rejected because it rewrites `right` links during a read-only walk. By `sizeof` (gcc 15.2, x86-64), `struct rb_node` is 48 bytes with the pointer, 40 without. Slots round up to 16, so both give a 48-byte stride and 85 nodes per slab (measured with `rb_pool_geometry`): in pooled mode the pointer is free, by accident of layout rather than design. In ordinary mode glibc 2.43's `malloc_usable_size` reports 56 bytes for the 48-byte node and 40 for the 40-byte one; that is usable size only, not glibc's per-chunk bookkeeping, and another allocator could differ. `pool_stats` counts objects, so it needed no change. We kept the pointer because deletion fixup has depended on it since HW1.

**Testing limits.** `make stress-asan` runs 10^6 nodes, balanced and as one left spine, heap and pooled, with `rb_foreach` and `rb_destroy` on a 64 KB thread stack. The routine Valgrind gate (`make memcheck`) uses 20,000 nodes because Valgrind is much slower; that shrink is deliberate. DEVLOG records a one-off scratch Valgrind run of the full 10^6 case that was also clean, but it is not a Makefile target.

The balanced million-node stress test alone cannot detect the recursive-stack problem; the adversarial left spine does. In a scratch copy (not committed), `rb_destroy` was replaced with a textbook recursive free and run under ASan. In heap mode the balanced tree passed at 20,000 and 10^6 nodes (a red-black tree's height is about 40), while the left spine, built by a test hook using the real rotations, overflowed the 64 KB stack at both sizes. The abort ended the run before the pooled cases, so the control was observed in heap mode only.

All four targets passed on this laptop, and `git status --short` is empty, so no tracked files changed. These are the results observed here this session, not DEVLOG's figures. I stopped after verification and did not build the archive.

## Pre-check
- **Sync:** `git fetch` ran with no errors. `main` is 3 commits ahead of `origin/main` and 0 behind, so `1d09840`, `93d01ae` and `35a9afc` are not pushed.
- **Working tree:** clean.
- **Tools:** gcc 15.2 and valgrind 3.26.0.

## Results

| Target | Exit | Assertions | Fuzzer | Sanitizer or Valgrind |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `make test` (about 9.7 s) | 0 | 5439 PASS, 0 FAIL: 5403 in the default run plus 36 in `--stress 20000` | 10^5 ops OK in heap and pooled | none run |
| `make asan` (clean ASan/UBSan rebuild, then the same test chain) | 0 | 5439 PASS, 0 FAIL | 10^5 ops OK in heap and pooled | no ASan, UBSan or LeakSanitizer reports |
| `make stress-asan` (about 30 s) | 0 | 36 PASS, 0 FAIL, "All stress tests passed (N=1000000)" | none run | no sanitizer reports |
| `make memcheck` (about 33 s) | 0 | default run "All tests passed"; stress run "All stress tests passed (N=20000)" | 2×10^4 ops OK in heap and pooled | 4 valgrind runs, each with ERROR SUMMARY 0 errors, "All heap blocks were freed" |

**Valgrind detail**
- **`test_rbtree`:** 7,806 allocs and 7,806 frees.
- **`fuzz` heap:** 20,108 allocs and 20,108 frees.
- **`fuzz` pooled:** 15,593 allocs and 15,593 frees.
- **`--stress 20000`:** 120,484 allocs and 120,484 frees.

## 64 KB stack
The million-node run ran on a 64 KB pthread stack. All four cases (heap and pooled, balanced and left spine) each passed "thread stack set to exactly 64 KB" and "worker thread created and joined". Also, `rb_foreach` and `rb_destroy` made no `rb_malloc` call, and each case visited all 10^6 keys in order.

## Caveats
- **Match with earlier docs:** every count matches what DEVLOG and CLAUDE.md recorded (5439 / 5403 / 36 / the four valgrind alloc counts). That's observed here, not assumed.
- **Fuzzer seeds:** the fuzzer used `time(NULL)` seeds (for example 1792006286), so these runs don't replay the desktop's seeds.
- **Million-node case:** it ran under ASan only. `make memcheck` still uses 20,000 nodes, as documented.
- **What was run:** I counted PASS and FAIL lines from the logs, and I didn't diff individual assertion names.
- **Logs:** the raw logs are in the session scratchpad, outside the repo.
